title: CLO 2025 Academic Month: 3D Empowerment, Upgrading Industry Talent Development
description: CLO 2025 Official Academic Monthly Course Review Now Available! Professor Li Yanmei from Shanghai University of Engineering Science guides you through the pain points of the traditional apparel industry and the importance of cultivating 3D talent for industry development and transformation.
transcript:
How to use 3D and 3D design?  
I want to discuss a few parts.  
The first two are about why we use 3D and 3D design.  
I think many teachers and classmates in our group are also using it, so everyone may understand this part better.  
Maybe the focus is still on parts 3 and 4, which include some designs we have in talent training and some small achievements we have taught, presented as a whole display.  

So why do we need this 3D?  
We all know that traditional clothing production has a long cycle, high cost, and constant modifications. Design innovation has also encountered some bottlenecks, especially now with many houses and buildings.  
In addition, in our entire industry, the small unit quick-release customization mode and pre-sale mode presented are actually very common.  
I think everyone is very clear about this, just turn it over.  

Therefore, the demand for clothing design talents is now very obvious.  
One is not only to have design creativity but also not just traditional structural craftsmanship. It must be designer technology.  
What about this technology?  
In the current industry, after so many years of development, I think a very obvious one is 3D.  
From the earliest time when everyone didn’t know it well to slowly getting to know it, in recent years it has become a must-have ability.  

So I think this includes the 3D clothing designers we have been talking about in the past two years, digital designers, and so on. Some new positions have been launched, becoming a new driving force for talent demand in the entire clothing industry.  
So for teaching, it also raises a very obvious demand.  

In general, in addition to traditional skills, many traditional designers are now also learning 3D.  
As the first step of the school to train people, such as college students and some graduate students before they enter society, we still hope they can master this skill.  
So in terms of job integration and the training of complementary talents, more work may have to be done.  

Then the entire virtual design—this is something everyone may have seen before.  
This was actually an experiment we did previously, showing that after using 3D, there is an improvement in overall design efficiency and unlimited expression of creativity.  
In addition, it has an environmental sustainability effect, so visualization can be achieved in our entire design process.  

The most obvious is the simulation of sewing effects, especially the simulation of fabric properties.  
But here, we may also—I'm not sure about others, but in our live broadcasts, some teachers and students have similar problems.  

In fact, what we encounter in teaching is a more obvious problem:  
Students may pay more attention to whether the effect of their design has been realized, whether the outer outline of the dress is realized, but there is no special attention to the properties of the fabric.  
So I think this is a relatively weak point in our current teaching.  

Then, from the modeling effect, achieving this is also part of our experience.  
That is, after students do 3D modeling, their understanding of structure and craftsmanship is actually promoted because they can feel it clearly.  

Previously, when learning samples, one might not know what the sample looks like just from hand drawing. Many schools do not know the appearance and have to make it out of craftsmanship, but not necessarily all do it.  
Especially in structure, it can be very abstract. But in three dimensions, when doing it, it is very intuitive to see what it actually looks like.  
So this is a big help for other courses.  

Regarding fabric, for example in our clothing material classes, there can be interaction, but we also recognize that currently this aspect is relatively weak.  

In actual application, it is mainly design sharing and the connection of five departments in e-commerce sections for sales. There are also many applications, including some of our practical work or pre-sales we are doing now. All can be done using 3D.  

Besides what we just talked about, the sample is a link between the sample and promotion, which we understand more deeply.  

In its application, new product development is involved.  
In our daily teaching, there are also some series designs, creative clothing designs, clothing development, fashion matching and layering, virtual windows, virtual stores, and some pre-sale designs and sales.  

Furthermore, many scenes we have seen can be realized now: digital humans, digital clothing, digital scenes—completely virtual.  
We also have some traditional clothes in the market undergoing this kind of reconstruction, including 3D clothing museums, and so on.  

Regarding software applications, everyone is basically familiar. We summarize six models:  
- Human model  
- Insert the sample  
- Mix  
- Three virtual  
- Adjust the fabric  
- Processing details  

Then, looking at our own school and some designs, because we started very early, our school first developed a professional direction.  

In 2003, this professional direction was a bit confusing but eventually became an independent recruitment major called Clothing Design and Engineering (CDCM).  
Because of this profession, we started recruiting in 2004 as an independent recruitment professional class.  

Due to this profession's development, we connected more with many domestic and foreign digitized companies.  
One example is Li Ke Ge Bo (name unclear), formerly PJM, and many similar digitized companies with whom we communicate extensively.  

Overall, our professional design includes design, sample production, production process management, and soft manufacturing.  
In this field, digitalization, information, and related resources and technologies are introduced and reflected systematically in the entire course.  

We also have cooperation with digitized companies, including donations and strategic cooperation, to build a more complete digitalized fashion design or production laboratory like CED.  
We have soft manufacturing, a production line, ERP, and our three-dimensional virtual system integrated earlier.  

So in 2016, our school set a digitalized clothing direction under the CED profession.  
This profession has always been centered on fashion design projects, with traditional courses still basically reserved.  

We also include some computer courses, such as programming design and digitalized app development, to enhance students’ application ability and problem-solving skills in the industry.  

Recently, we combined the latest developments and opened courses in clothing app engineering applications, clothing data, clothing digital supply chain management, and so on.  
These courses closely relate to industry development.  

Our 3D virtual design and talent training started relatively early.  
We opened this major in 2004 and contacted 3D software companies as early as 2007, probably the earliest.  
Initially, we used the software mainly for related research, such as fabric properties.  

Around 2010, we gradually connected with these companies and offered some subjects and elective classes.  
In 2016, we deepened cooperation with companies and trained many people. Many former students now work in these companies.  

In 2018, we established a multiplied 3D virtual clothing design course, which I will discuss later.  
This year, we cooperated with our company to open a semi-professional and semi-classical statement.  

Overall, from education to design, we are multi-layered in teaching design.  
We developed a relatively comprehensive 3D course system based on our teaching plan for professional classes.  
This is mainly in the theoretical section focusing on basic functions.  

In the concentration time section, there is a course design that realizes case-by-case projects.  
When opened in recent years, this course is linked with a theoretical class called Brand Clothing Product Project.  
This project is a collaboration, covering both pre-release and post-release, which we will look at later through student works.  

The third part is creative expansion outside the class.  
We opened an innovative experimental project for related professional students, as well as an innovative practical class, which is like a second class event.  

This year, we opened micro-profession and micro-classes responding to our school’s overall micro-professional system, mainly extended to the industry.  
These reflect enterprise and industry needs and respond to school talent demands.  

For students, these are small workloads, about 12 to 18 credits, allowing quick skills improvement aligned with enterprise or industry needs.  
We issue micro-professional certificates, which are recognized by some enterprises as proof of study completion.  

We also actively recommend students for internships to help them perform better jobs.  

Through the previous comprehensive teaching design, we hope students at different levels can gain something.  

First is the basic layer, realized basically in professional classes.  
This lets students master basic modeling functions, basic tools, understand the transition between 2D and 3D mixing, paper adjustments, fabric texture, color settings, and other basic skills.  

All these basic courses are recorded and available on the learning channel as videos.  
In each part, based on version, we insert many videos from our own teaching group classes, so students can conveniently learn in and out of class.  

Although we have many listed classes, we actually have very few classes: two professional classes with 32 classes each, one-week concentration time equaling about 30 classes, and expansion courses with less than 20 classes.  

So within a limited number of classes, we want students to better master virtual design skills to create.  
We use many recorded courses carefully made, so students can basically learn without guidance.  

However, we encountered some problems in the past two years.  
In communication with our company, we found that our courses tend to focus more on transforming samples from 2D to 3D.  
Students are interested because it is intuitive to see their 2D design become 3D clothing visually, but they may overlook many internal details.  

This is one problem.  
Another limitation is our school’s equipment, affecting post-production effects, which are weaker.  
Sometimes, particle monitors are very small, and our computers have limited performance.  
So the overall rendering effect is weaker, which we consider a clear problem.  

The second is the advanced layer, where students emphasize different fabrics, clothing textures, and reflecting physical attributes, including sounds of clothes, distance, and vertical movement.  

Some students improve the overall accuracy of the board shape and fabric properties, aiming for higher quality.  
We hope students can apply this basic knowledge to their graduation designs, modify samples, refresh creativity, and achieve natural folds through fabric adjustments.  

We encourage students in design class to realize their graduation designs and also to show and plan some works in virtual fashion shows.  
Of course, as mentioned, due to equipment limitations, the effect is not particularly strong, which is a key point for us.  

In the application of teaching, we hope to apply 3D to various sections.  
For example, some market tools can be used in teaching brand fashion design and planning with timelines.  

In the fashion room teaching, we combine this with a digital museum.  
We also completed a virtual sewing experimental project of Ming Dynasty palace official costumes, a first-class city project in Shanghai, included in fashion room teaching.  

In combination with fashion engineering, we edited a project by a company that makes digital human masks.  
Traditionally, real people's masks were made, but recently digital human masks have developed, picking people worldwide and making masks according to different countries’ fashion styles.  

We combine this with human body measurement and clothing styles in public schools to do some combinations.  

We completed some cases in teaching mainly involving students.  
The intensive part is the one-week class mentioned earlier.  
This one-week course links with the brand clothing design and planning course.  

Because there are very few classes in my class, we hope the whole process from planning to effect rendering can be completed.  
So we use a previous course for planning cases and realize the effect in 3D, including atmosphere boards, color boards, design ideas, and fabric choices.  

This is one of the first meetings of engineering students, maybe the first draft of this work.  
They find relevant costumes and materials and do two homework assignments in this week.  

One is the first meeting realization in 3D, and the other is to find a related or different theme, such as food clothing, and realize and compare the effect in 3D.  

This is done individually, not in groups.  

One student completed his own handmade 3D realization of an early existing product.  
After this effect is done, he presents a show, which is relatively simple.  

We research problems and find what is visible on the desktop.  

The second point is that the weekly course topic changes every year.  
Last year, we coincided with a cheongsam (qipao) competition in our college and integrated the course with it, realizing some excellent works in 3D.  

Next, this sharing is about combining 3D with design specialization training.  
One student designed an innovative seaside cheongsam, from design draft to 3D realization to the final complete work.  

Also, in undergraduate graduation design, some works use 3D.  
Last year, a student did a digital display of ethnic minority clothing, creating a series of products and a simple building model.  
Graduation design time is short, making it hard to complete more.  

Additionally, we have a virtual innovative design practice course for evening gowns with about 20 students.  
This course is shorter, about five weeks, and many students are cross-disciplinary, so we use recorded videos for instruction.  

We push students to learn a lot outside class.  
The operation method is that after learning basic functions, many cross-disciplinary students without design ability use existing evening gowns, including some from online runway shows, to realize the gown effect in 3D and compare fabric patterns.  

We grade based on implementation degree and overall completion.  

We also use 3D as an auxiliary tool in public school research, including undergraduate and graduate students.  

For example, one student working on a project about breathing analyzed pressure from different angles in 3D, mapping muscle pressure distribution, correlating real and virtual data.  

Over the years, 3D has promoted our scientific research.  
Teachers have received Shanghai Art Fund and Ministry of Education Humanities and Social Science Fund, focusing on 3D in traditional clothing restoration and preservation.  

Last year, Shanghai had an AI project on deep-level AI-generated clothing design, which we participated in.  

During these projects, there is reciprocal teaching; for example, research on Ming Dynasty official costumes is included in graduation theses.  
Students also do innovative Hanfu graduation designs.  

In teaching, we have Shanghai first-class courses and related curriculum projects that clearly promote student employment and meet industry needs.  

In recent years, employment in this field has increased, including many of our students working at Koro Company (our mentioned company).  

From application trends, many can now clearly experience 3D integration with AI and other technologies like VR and AR.  

This year, we applied for a micro-professional program called AIJC Digital Virtual Fashion Design and another called Virtual Clothing Innovation Design.  
We also explore integration with virtual reality technologies and online digital twin displays, leaving space for further exploration in teaching.  

Another deep insight from teaching is the need for more industry integration and communication.  

Previously, our company communicated frequently with us, and we always felt the biggest pain point was that although we teach students a lot, we do not fully understand the detailed skill requirements of enterprises for specific positions.  

We know there is demand for these positions, but the detailed skill requirements are unclear to us.  

So maybe to promote student employment and help them solve practical problems, we need more work integrating with the industry in the future.  

Overall, after many years of lectures, practical operations, and cases, we see good effects.  
Feedback from students and our teaching team is positive.  

Some student works are more complete, especially in skills.  
Many students are confident and enjoy it, which also promotes employment.  

What is lacking?  
More obvious is the limitation of our software and hardware, which affects rendering and effect details.  

Also, in actual teaching time, student control varies significantly; in the same class, some students progress quickly and do very well, others struggle, which is a headache.  

Ultimately, results vary, but we hope all students can have a good experience in actual teaching.  

Thank you very much.  
Thank you very much.  
Thank you very much.  

I also hope that in the future I can reach a similar level of understanding and explore this area more in subsequent teaching.  

Overall, this is what I wanted to share. Thank you, everyone.

chunks.title: CLO 2025 Academic Month: 3D Empowerment, Upgrading Industry Talent Development
chunks.content: ## Introduction to 3D and 3D Design in Clothing Industry This section explains the significance of 3D technology and 3D design in modern clothing production and talent development. It highlights the limitations of traditional methods and the increasing industry demand for technologically skilled designers. Traditional clothing production faces challenges such as long development cycles, high costs, and frequent modifications. Design innovation has also encountered bottlenecks, especially in the context of rapid customization and pre-sale models common in the industry. The demand for clothing design talent now emphasizes not only creativity but also technological proficiency, particularly in 3D design. 3D design has evolved from an unfamiliar tool to an essential skill in the clothing industry. New roles like 3D clothing designers and digital designers have emerged, becoming a driving force behind talent requirements. Consequently, educational institutions aim to integrate 3D skills into their curricula to equip students—college and graduate levels—with competencies that align with industry needs. ## Advantages of 3D Virtual Design in Education and Industry This section covers the benefits of 3D virtual design in improving design efficiency, creativity, sustainability, and educational outcomes, along with the current challenges in teaching fabric properties and realistic simulation. Using 3D design enhances overall design efficiency and allows unlimited creative expression. It supports environmental sustainability by enabling visualization throughout the design process without physical sampling. The most significant technical advantage is realistic simulation of sewing effects and fabric properties. However, student attention tends to focus more on the dress silhouette and less on fabric characteristics, indicating a teaching gap. The 3D modeling process improves students’ understanding of structure and craftsmanship by providing intuitive, three-dimensional views of garments that are difficult to grasp through hand drawings or abstract concepts. Fabric interaction remains a weak point in current education, though it is addressed somewhat in clothing materials courses. In practical applications, 3D is used for design sharing, coordination among e-commerce departments, pre-sales, and new product development. Virtual stores, digital humans, and 3D clothing museums illustrate the expanding scope of 3D applications. ## 3D Software Applications and Teaching Models This section summarizes the core software functionalities used in 3D clothing design and introduces the school’s pioneering role in 3D design education, including industry cooperation. Six primary software modules are commonly utilized: - Human modeling - Sample insertion - Mixing 2D and 3D elements - Three-dimensional virtual simulation - Fabric adjustment - Processing detail refinement The school began professional training in Clothing Design and Engineering (CDCM) in 2003, formalizing an independent major by 2004. It established partnerships with domestic and international digital fashion companies to enhance curriculum relevance and resource availability. The curriculum integrates design, sample production, production process management, and soft manufacturing, reflecting digitalization and information technologies systematically. Collaboration with companies includes donations, strategic cooperation, and the establishment of digital fashion laboratories incorporating ERP and advanced virtual systems.

chunks.title: CLO 2025 Academic Month: 3D Empowerment, Upgrading Industry Talent Development
chunks.content: Six primary software modules are commonly utilized: - Human modeling - Sample insertion - Mixing 2D and 3D elements - Three-dimensional virtual simulation - Fabric adjustment - Processing detail refinement The school began professional training in Clothing Design and Engineering (CDCM) in 2003, formalizing an independent major by 2004. It established partnerships with domestic and international digital fashion companies to enhance curriculum relevance and resource availability. The curriculum integrates design, sample production, production process management, and soft manufacturing, reflecting digitalization and information technologies systematically. Collaboration with companies includes donations, strategic cooperation, and the establishment of digital fashion laboratories incorporating ERP and advanced virtual systems. ## Curriculum Development and 3D Talent Training This section explains the evolution of the 3D-focused curriculum, the layering of courses, and the integration of theoretical and practical training to meet industry demands. Since 2004, the school has progressively developed courses in 3D virtual design, starting with research on fabric properties and expanding to electives by 2010. A significant development came in 2016 with deeper industry cooperation, leading to widespread employment of graduates in digital fashion companies. The curriculum features multiple layers: - **Basic Layer:** Focuses on foundational skills such as modeling, 2D-3D transitions, fabric textures, and color settings. Recorded video lessons support self-paced learning. - **Advanced Layer:** Emphasizes detailed fabric and texture simulation, physical clothing attributes (including sound and movement), and higher-quality rendering. - **Creative Expansion:** Includes innovative experimental projects, micro-professional courses (12-18 credits), and industry-aligned training with certification recognized by enterprises. A one-week intensive course links brand clothing design with 3D realization, involving individual assignments that challenge students to transform design ideas into 3D models. The course evolves annually, sometimes aligning with college competitions, such as a cheongsam (qipao) design contest. ## Practical Applications and Student Projects This section details practical teaching applications, student work examples, and interdisciplinary integration involving 3D design. Students use 3D to realize designs from drafts to final products, including innovative ethnic minority clothing and evening gowns. Cross-disciplinary students utilize existing gown designs and online runway examples to practice 3D implementation. 3D tools also support public school research projects, such as analyzing breathing and muscle pressure distribution through 3D mapping, linking real and virtual data. Teachers have secured funding for projects focused on traditional clothing restoration and preservation using 3D technology. The school also supports virtual sewing projects, digital human mask development, and digital museums, integrating historical costumes with advanced technology. ## Industry Collaboration and Employment Outcomes This section discusses the school's engagement with industry, the challenges in aligning education with enterprise skill requirements, and the positive impact on student employment. The school maintains active communication with digital fashion companies but recognizes a gap in fully understanding detailed enterprise skill demands for specific roles. Addressing this gap is essential for improving student employability and practical problem-solving abilities. Feedback from students and teaching staff is positive, with many students demonstrating confidence and skill proficiency that support job placement.

chunks.title: CLO 2025 Academic Month: 3D Empowerment, Upgrading Industry Talent Development
chunks.content: ## Industry Collaboration and Employment Outcomes This section discusses the school's engagement with industry, the challenges in aligning education with enterprise skill requirements, and the positive impact on student employment. The school maintains active communication with digital fashion companies but recognizes a gap in fully understanding detailed enterprise skill demands for specific roles. Addressing this gap is essential for improving student employability and practical problem-solving abilities. Feedback from students and teaching staff is positive, with many students demonstrating confidence and skill proficiency that support job placement. However, hardware and software limitations constrain rendering quality, and student progress varies significantly within classes. Recent trends show integration of 3D with AI, VR, and AR technologies. The school has launched micro-professional programs such as AIJC Digital Virtual Fashion Design and Virtual Clothing Innovation Design, exploring virtual reality and digital twin displays. ## Challenges and Future Directions This section outlines current limitations in equipment and teaching methods, the variability in student learning outcomes, and plans for enhancing industry integration and technical capabilities. Key challenges include limited computing performance and small particle monitors affecting rendering quality. These hardware constraints impede post-production effects and detailed visualization. Student skill levels vary widely, creating difficulties in uniform teaching outcomes. The school aims to provide a consistent and positive learning experience for all students. Future efforts will focus on deeper industry collaboration to clarify skill requirements, improving hardware infrastructure, and expanding curriculum offerings integrating AI, VR, and other emerging technologies. The goal is to enhance the relevance and effectiveness of 3D talent development aligned with industry evolution.
